ALMA Chemical Evolution (ACE) Survey: Molecular gas properties of low-mass, low-metallicity galaxies at cosmic noon

Abstract

Molecular gas plays a central role in regulating star formation and galaxy evolution, yet observational constraints at cosmic noon remain biased toward massive, metal-rich systems. We present ALMA Band 3 observations of the CO J=3J=3–2 transition in 26 unlensed star-forming galaxies from the ALMA Chemical Evolution (ACE) Large Program at z∼2z\sim 2–2.5, probing stellar masses of 109≲M⋆≲1010.5​M⊙10^{9}\lesssim M_{\star}\lesssim 10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} and sub-solar metallicities (8.2<12+log⁡(O/H)<8.68.2<12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})<8.6). We derived molecular gas masses using a metallicity-dependent CO-to-H2 conversion factor and alongside analysed stacking measurements and a homogenized literature compilation spanning both local and high-redshift galaxies. We find that the ACE galaxies extend established molecular-gas scaling relations to an order of magnitude lower stellar masses than previously explored at cosmic noon. The molecular gas mass (MmolM_{\rm mol}) correlates tightly with star formation rate (SFR), while molecular gas fractions show a strong dependence on specific star formation rate (sSFR) and offset from the star-forming main sequence. In contrast, molecular gas fractions show only weak trends with stellar mass and no significant dependence on metallicity. Molecular gas depletion times are ∼1​Gyr\sim 1\,\mathrm{Gyr} and vary little with stellar mass or metallicity, and weakly with sSFR and offset from the star-forming main sequence. Together this further reinforces that the availability of molecular gas is the primary driver of the SFR in galaxies, with changes in star-formation efficiency playing a secondary role. Leveraging the expanded parameter space probed by the ACE and literature samples, we derive a new empirical prescription for predicting MmolM_{\rm mol} as a function of SFR and sSFR. The persistence of the observed scaling relations across a broader range of galaxy properties than probed before at cosmic noon suggests a largely universal framework governing the molecular gas–star formation cycle across cosmic time.

Key Words.
galaxies: high-redshift – galaxies: evolution – galaxies: ISM - galaxies: formation

1 Introduction

Molecular gas is the fuel that drives star formation and galaxy evolution across cosmic time. Understanding the mechanisms that regulate how molecular gas is converted into stars remains a key goal in astrophysics. In the framework of the baryon cycle through galaxies, a galaxy’s star formation rate (SFR\mathrm{SFR}) is determined by a continuous balance between gas accretion from the cosmic web, star formation, and stellar-driven outflows (Bouché et al., 2010; Davé et al., 2012; Lilly et al., 2013, e.g.,). Within this paradigm, the molecular gas reservoir acts as the central engine. Scaling relations that link global galaxy properties – like stellar mass (M⋆M_{\star}, star-formation rate (SFR), and redshift (z) – to molecular gas properties – like molecular gas mass (MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}), molecular-to-stellar mass ratio (Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}), gas depletion time (tdep≡Mmol/SFRt_{\mathrm{dep}}\equiv M_{\mathrm{mol}}/\mathrm{SFR}) – offer a direct look into the physics regulating this cycle, showing how galaxies grow along the star-forming main sequence (Noeske et al., 2007; Elbaz et al., 2010, SFMS;).

The redshift range z∼1z\sim 1–33 represents a particularly significant epoch in the history of the Universe, corresponding to the peak of cosmic star formation activity, often referred to as “cosmic noon” (Madau and Dickinson, 2014). Galaxies during this period formed stars at rates substantially higher than those observed in the local Universe. Massive galaxies had elevated gas fractions, enhanced star-formation efficiencies, and distinct interstellar medium (ISM) conditions, highlighting the need for direct observations of representative cosmic noon galaxy populations (Steidel et al., 2014; Kaasinen et al., 2017; Tacconi et al., 2018; Aravena et al., 2019). Testing the scaling relations that connect cold-gas content to stellar mass assembly at these redshifts is therefore essential for understanding the mechanisms that regulate galaxy growth and drive the peak of cosmic star formation.

Over the past decade, observational surveys with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), Plateau de Bure Interferometer (PDBI), and Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) have revolutionized our view of the molecular gas in cosmic noon galaxies. By using both CO\mathrm{CO} line transitions and dust continuum emission as gas tracers, these surveys have established robust empirical scaling relations for the molecular gas content of galaxies across a range of redshifts, stellar masses, and SFRs (Tacconi et al., 2013; Genzel et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2017; Tacconi et al., 2018; Aravena et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Tacconi et al., 2020; Gómez-Guijarro et al., 2022; Sanders et al., 2023, e.g.,). These relations provide relevant constraints for the baryon cycle and indicate that a galaxy’s location relative to the SFMS is tightly coupled to the availability of cold molecular gas.

The star formation efficiency (SFE\mathrm{SFE}) of galaxies is fundamentally regulated by localized physical conditions, rooted in cloud-scale densities and turbulent pressure and feedback from young stars and supernovae (Ostriker and Kim, 2022). These cloud properties, however, are shaped by the broader, large-scale dynamics of the galactic disk. This connection between small-scale star-forming environments and disk-scale structure is often parameterized in terms of gravitational stability via the Toomre QQ parameter (Genzel et al., 2011; Wisnioski et al., 2015, e.g.,). Ultimately, these localized variations scale up to determine the integrated gas depletion timescales (tdep=Mmol/SFRt_{\mathrm{dep}}=M_{\rm mol}/\rm{SFR}), which previous surveys have shown to evolve with cosmic time and with distance from the SFMS (Aravena et al., 2019; Tacconi et al., 2020).

Despite this progress, current observational samples of unlensed field galaxies suffer from strong selection biases. Although dust continuum measurements are highly efficient for targeting large samples, CO\mathrm{CO} line emission remains the most direct and physically robust way to trace the bulk molecular gas. However, existing unlensed CO\mathrm{CO} observations at high redshift are heavily skewed toward massive (M⋆≳1010.5​M⊙M_{\star}\gtrsim 10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}) and metal-rich (approximately solar metallicity) systems (Hodge and da Cunha, 2020; Tacconi et al., 2020, for recent reviews see). Because of this, we still lack a clear empirical picture of the molecular gas cycle in typical low-mass, low-metallicity galaxies at cosmic noon, even though these systems are the direct progenitors of Milky Way-like galaxies today. Moreover, most CO-observed galaxies lack the gas-phase metallicity measurements needed to robustly estimate the CO-to-H2 conversion factor (Narayanan et al., 2012; Bolatto et al., 2013).

To push toward low stellar masses (M⋆≲1010.5​M⊙M_{\star}\lesssim 10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}) and low-metallicity (12+log⁡(O/H)<8.612+\log{(O/H)}<8.6) systems, observations have traditionally relied on the flux-boosting power of strong gravitational lensing (Saintonge et al., 2013; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Motta et al., 2018; Solimano, 2022; Catán et al., 2024; Tsujita et al., 2025, e.g.,). Although these pioneering lensing campaigns provide an invaluable look into the low-mass regime, they are intrinsically limited by small, stochastic samples that carry complex lens modelling and structural reconstruction uncertainties. Crucially, what is lacking is a statistically representative sample of unlensed low-mass sources selected with clear, uniform criteria and backed by wide ancillary data, for which molecular gas and metallicity information is available.

The current lack of observations stands in contrast to theoretical models, which are already well-developed. Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations and semi-analytic models have advanced significantly, incorporating detailed treatments for the multi-phase ISM (Obreschkow et al., 2009; Lagos et al., 2011; Popping et al., 2014; Popping et al., 2015; Lagos et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2017; Popping et al., 2019; Davé et al., 2020; Lagos et al., 2026, e.g.,). These models make explicit predictions for the molecular gas properties of galaxies over cosmic time. They find that galaxies were more gas rich at cosmic noon than in the local universe and their molecular-to-stellar mass ratio decreases with increasing stellar mass (Popping et al., 2015, e.g.,). Lagos et al. (2026) furthermore finds a positive correlation between molecular gas depletion time and metallicity on resolved scales and that at fixed metallicities the depletion time increases with time. Testing these predictions requires expanding our observational boundaries into the low-mass, metal-poor regime using well-understood selection functions across cosmic time.

In this paper, we present the molecular gas content of galaxies observed as part of the ALMA Chemical Evolution (ACE) survey, an ALMA Large Program designed to bridge this observational gap. ACE targets the CO J==3–2 emission line in unlensed z=2−2.5z=2-2.5 galaxies with stellar masses nearly an order of magnitude lower (109<M⋆<1010.5​M⊙10^{9}<M_{\star}<10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}) and gas-phase metallicities roughly 0.4​dex0.4\,\mathrm{dex} lower (8.2<12+log⁡(O/H)<8.68.2<12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})<8.6) than previous unlensed CO\mathrm{CO} samples. Crucially, this program pairs these new CO\mathrm{CO} observations with robust gas-phase metallicity measurements based on strong nebular emission lines and a wide suite of multi-wavelength ancillary data (Shivaei et al., 2026). This unique combination allows us to establish a clearer view of molecular gas scaling relations and how cold gas reservoirs shape galaxy assembly in a lower mass and lower metallicity regime than has been possible until now.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present the ACE sample, the ALMA Band 3 CO J==3–2 observations, and the literature data used for comparison. In Section 3, we describe our methods for measuring CO\mathrm{CO} line fluxes and converting them into molecular gas masses. We present our results in Section 4, discuss their implications in Section 5, and summarize our main findings in Section 6. Throughout this work, we assume a Chabrier (2003) initial mass function (IMF) and adopt a Planck Collaboration et al. (2020) cosmology with H0=67.66​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=67.66\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}, Ωm=0.3111\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}=0.3111, and ΩΛ=0.6889\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.6889. Metallicity is defined in terms of the gas-phase oxygen abundance, 12+log⁡(O/H)12+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H}), and throughout the paper we adopt a solar metallicity of 12+log⁡(O/H)⊙=8.6912+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H})_{\odot}=8.69 (Asplund et al., 2009). All presented molecular gas masses include a contribution from helium and metals.

2 Sample and Observations

2.1 ACE sample selection and properties

The primary sample analyzed in this work is drawn from the ALMA large program ACE (2024.1.00534.L), which targets a subset of the star-forming galaxies (SFGs) at z∼2.0​–​2.5z\sim 2.0\text{--}2.5, previously characterized in Shivaei et al. (2022). These sources were originally selected from the MOSFIRE Deep Evolution Field (MOSDEF) survey (Kriek et al., 2015), comprising ∼1500\sim 1500 galaxies with Keck/MOSFIRE near-infrared (NIR) spectra. Shivaei et al. (2022) presented 1.2​mm1.2\,\mathrm{mm} dust continuum measurements for 2727 typical main-sequence SFGs. The ACE large program has built a sample of 2525 of these galaxies with measurements of the CO J==3–2 emission line, 3​mm3\,\mathrm{mm}, and 1​mm1\,\mathrm{mm} dust continuum emission. We use the 22 ACE galaxies targeted in ALMA band 3 (the remaining 3 galaxies being only targeted in ALMA band 7) and an additional 4 galaxies with ALMA band 3 CO J==3–2 detections from Sanders et al. (2023), totaling 26 galaxies (one on top of the ACE sample of 25, but with the exact same available ancillary information). Because the ACE sample is located within the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field (Scoville et al., 2007), we leverage the extensive multi-wavelength photometry available (e.g., from the 3D-HST survey; Skelton et al. 2014), supplemented by new James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) NIRCam and MIRI data from the COSMOS2025 (Casey et al., 2023; Shuntov et al., 2025) and PRIMER (Dunlop et al., 2021) programs. Using this photometric baseline and our ALMA continuum observations (Popescu et al., 2026), in Shivaei et al. (2026) we derive stellar masses (M⋆M_{\star}) and SFR\mathrm{SFR}s averaged over 10​Myr10\,\mathrm{Myr} via spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting with the Prospector code (Leja et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2021). We assume a delayed-τ\tau star formation history with a flat age prior between 1 Myr and the age of the universe at the redshift of the galaxy. In Shivaei et al. (2026) we furthermore determined gas-phase metallicities from multiple rest-frame optical and NIR emission lines (spanning [OII]​λ​λ​3726,3729[\mathrm{OII}]\lambda\lambda 3726,3729 to [SII]​λ​λ​6716,6731[\mathrm{SII}]\lambda\lambda 6716,6731; Kriek et al. 2015) adopting the strong-line calibrations of Sanders et al. (2026). The final sample spans a range of 9.13<log⁡(M∗/M⊙)<10.629.13<\log(M_{*}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})<10.62 and 1.3<log⁡(SFR/M⊙​yr−1)<2.21.3<\log(\mathrm{SFR}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1})<2.2 and metallicities from 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.1912+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=8.19 to 8.61. The derived properties of the ACE targets are listed in Table 2. More details on the SED-fitting, metallicity estimation, and sample characteristics are provided in Shivaei et al. (2026).

We note that other ACE studies have adopted star-formation rates (SFRs) derived from Hα\alpha emission and corrected for dust attenuation using the Balmer decrement. In this work, however, we use SFRs obtained from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting (see Shivaei et al. 2026 for the SED fitting details), as Hα\alpha-based SFR measurements are not available for the literature comparison sample (Section 2.3). Adopting SED-based SFRs therefore enables the most consistent comparison between the two samples.

2.2 ALMA Band 3 CO J==3–2 observations

The ALMA Band 3 CO J==3–2 observational setup, data calibration, imaging, and flux measurement strategies are presented in detail in Langan et al. (2026) and Shivaei et al. (2026). Below, we briefly summarize the adopted approaches, but we refer the reader to the aforementioned papers for more detailed descriptions. The described approaches were applied to the targets observed as part of the ACE Large Program, as well as the archival datasets originally presented in Sanders et al. (2023).

We make use of calibrated measurement sets provided by the European ALMA Regional Centre through the calMS service (Petry et al., 2020). For the imaging of the data, we make use of the Common Astronomy Software Applications (CASA v6.5.21; CASATeam et al. 2022) package. We use the tclean task with natural weighting (𝚛𝚘𝚋𝚞𝚜𝚝=𝟸\mathtt{robust=2}) to create cubes, with a channel width of Δ​v=7.8125​MHz\Delta v=7.8125\,\mathrm{MHz} (∼23​km​s−1\sim 23\,\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}). This provides an optimal balance between the signal-to-noise ratio (S/NS/N) and the sampling of the line profile. The aim of the ACE program is to fully recover the CO J==3–2 line flux of the sources. To this end, we generated data cubes at the native resolution as well as with 1​″1\arcsec and 2​″2\arcsec u​vuv-tapering. We next defined a scoring function consisting of the product of the integrated flux and the peak S/NS/N for each image to evaluate which of these images is best suited to recover the total flux of the source within a single beam element. The image with the highest score (among the native resolution, 1​″1\arcsec, and 2​″2\arcsec tapering, respectively) was used for subsequent analysis. Each selection was visually inspected against JWST imaging to prevent flux contamination from neighboring sources. We refer the reader to Langan et al. (2026) for a more detailed description.

The derivation of optimized CO J==3–2 moment-0 images and spectra followed an iterative procedure also presented in Langan et al. (2026). Initially, we collapsed the data cubes over a velocity range corresponding to the Hα\alpha full-width-half-maximum (Kriek et al., 2015) around the systemic redshift. From this preliminary image, we identified the emission peak and extracted a 1D spectrum, which was then fitted to determine the CO\mathrm{CO} line width. This width was subsequently used to define the velocity interval for the final, optimized moment-0 image. As a final step, we extracted the CO J==3–2 spectrum from the peak pixel of this optimized image.

2.3 Literature datasets

2.3.1 z=2−2.5z=2-2.5 literature compilation with metallicity and CO information

We complement our ACE sample with literature data at similar redshifts from the Plateau de Bure High-zz Blue Sequence Survey (Tacconi et al., 2013; Tacconi et al., 2018, PHIBSS;) and ALMA Spectroscopic Survey in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field (Aravena et al., 2019; González-López et al., 2019; Boogaard et al., 2019; Boogaard et al., 2020, ASPECS;). These literature galaxies are selected based on the availability of molecular gas measurements derived from CO\mathrm{CO} observations, as well as the availability of optical strong lines observed through either ground-based or JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy (after cross-matching to the DAWN JWST Archive spectroscopic release; Valentino et al. 2025; Pollock et al. 2026), alongside complementary JWST/NIRCam coverage. This results in 8 galaxies from ASPECS and 6 galaxies from PHIBSS. Nine of these galaxies roughly fall within our target redshift range of z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5. To ensure a self-consistent analysis, we derived the M⋆M_{\star} and SFR\mathrm{SFR} for these targets by applying the previously mentioned SED-fitting methodology explained in Shivaei et al. (2026), and their metallicities using the Sanders et al. (2026) calibration adopted for the ACE galaxies. Molecular gas masses (MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}) are derived using the exact same assumption for the CO-to-H2 conversion factor and CO(3–2) to CO(1–0) excitation correction as those applied to the ACE targets (see Section 3).

In many of the figures throughout this paper, we also include the compilation of galaxies at z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5 with CO\mathrm{CO}-based molecular gas masses presented in the review by Tacconi et al. (2020, including lensed and unlensed galaxies). We adopt the molecular hydrogen masses exactly as presented in the Tacconi et al. (2020) compilation, which assume a constant CO\mathrm{CO}-to-H2\mathrm{H}_{2} conversion factor of αCO=4.6​M⊙​(K​km​s−1​pc2)−1\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}}=4.6\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,(\mathrm{K}\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{pc}^{2})^{-1}, as we lack metallicity information to rescale them to the Accurso et al. (2017) conversion factor. We include this compilation to place our results in the context of the extensive literature that has set the standard in the field; however, we note that the molecular gas masses derived in this work for the ACE sample and our new literature compilation are more robust, given that they account for the explicit dependence of the CO\mathrm{CO}-to-H2\mathrm{H}_{2} conversion factor on measured metallicities.

2.3.2 z=0z=0 compilation

To place our findings in the context of local galaxies, we compare the ACE sample to the z=0z=0 galaxy compilation from Galliano et al. (2021), focusing specifically on sources with secure CO\mathrm{CO} detections. This local sample spans a significantly wider metallicity range than alternative low-redshift compilations, making it an ideal baseline for comparison with the low-metallicity regime probed by ACE. Because a subset of sources in the Galliano et al. (2021) parent catalog lacked CO\mathrm{CO}-based molecular gas information, we cross-matched their compilation with the sample from Colombo et al. (2025) to supplement the missing CO\mathrm{CO} fluxes where available. This cross-matching yields a final local comparison sample of 143 galaxies. For a consistent comparison, we recalculate the molecular gas masses for this local sample adopting the same CO\mathrm{CO}-to-H2\mathrm{H}_{2} conversion factor methodology described in Section 3.

3 CO line flux measurement and molecular gas mass estimation

The derivation of CO J==3–2 line properties and integrated fluxes is based on the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Gaussian fitting procedure described in detail in Langan et al. (2026). Briefly, we generated 50005000 noise realizations for each spectrum by perturbing the data with Gaussian noise scaled to the local 𝑟𝑚𝑠\mathit{rms} level. Each realization was fitted with a single Gaussian profile to determine the median integrated flux, FintF_{\mathrm{int}}, and the associated kinematic parameters. For sources with S/N<4\mathrm{S/N}<4, we repeated the fitting procedure by fixing the Gaussian width to the corresponding H​α\mathrm{H}\alpha line width (FWHMH​α\mathrm{FWHM}_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}; Kriek et al. 2015), accounting for the respective spectral resolutions.

We adopted a conservative estimate for the flux uncertainties, defined as the maximum of the standard deviation from the MCMC realizations and the noise-based estimate, 𝑟𝑚𝑠av×Nchan×Δ​v\mathit{rms}_{\mathrm{av}}\times\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{chan}}}\times\Delta v, where NchanN_{\mathrm{chan}} is the number of channels within the line 1​σ1\sigma width. Non-detections are defined as sources with an integrated flux S/N<3\mathrm{S/N}<3. For these objects, we adopt 3​σ3\sigma upper limits calculated as 3×𝑟𝑚𝑠av×Nchan×Δ​v3\times\mathit{rms}_{\mathrm{av}}\times\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{chan}}}\times\Delta v, where NchanN_{\mathrm{chan}} corresponds to the velocity interval of 2×FWHMH​α2\times\mathrm{FWHM}_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}. In total, our sample consists of 1717 detections with a mean S/N≈5\mathrm{S/N}\approx 5 and 99 upper limits (Shivaei et al., 2026). The extracted CO J==3–2 flux densities are listed in Table 2.

To derive molecular gas masses from the CO(33–22) observations, we first convert the integrated line fluxes to CO(11–00) luminosities (LCO⁡(1−0)′L^{\prime}_{\mathrm{CO}(1-0)}) by adopting a line brightness temperature ratio of r31=LCO⁡(3−2)′/LCO⁡(1−0)′=0.77±0.14r_{31}=L^{\prime}_{\mathrm{CO}(3-2)}/L^{\prime}_{\mathrm{CO}(1-0)}=0.77\pm 0.14. This value is taken from Boogaard et al. (2020), who derived it from a stacking analysis of typical star-forming galaxies at z∼2.5z\sim 2.5. The adoption of this excitation correction is further supported by observations of local dwarf galaxies, which show no evidence for systematically different CO excitation conditions compared to more metal-rich systems (Meier et al., 2001; Cormier et al., 2014). Nevertheless, the CO excitation properties of low-mass, low-metallicity galaxies at high redshift remain largely unexplored observationally, and the applicability of this value in the regime probed by ACE has yet to be tested directly (see also Anirudh et al. 2025 for theoretical considerations).

The choice of the CO\mathrm{CO}-to-H2\mathrm{H}_{2} conversion factor (αCO=Mmol/LCO⁡(1−0)′\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}}=M_{\mathrm{mol}}/L^{\prime}_{\mathrm{CO}(1-0)}) is critical, as it is known to vary with gas-phase metallicity (Narayanan et al., 2012; Bolatto et al., 2013, e.g.,). To determine the most suitable CO-to-H2 conversion factor for our sample, Langan et al. (2026) used the dynamical mass method to obtain independent estimates of αCO\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}} from the observed CO line widths. These values were subsequently compared with several metallicity-dependent αCO\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}} prescriptions from the literature (Bolatto et al., 2013; Accurso et al., 2017; Madden et al., 2020, e.g.,). Langan et al. (2026) found that the dynamical estimates are in best agreement with the calibration presented in Accurso et al. (2017), which is subsequently the conversion used throughout the ACE papers.The resulting molecular gas masses, which include a contribution for Helium, are presented in Langan et al. (2026) and for clarity also listed in Table 2.

3.1 Stacking

Despite the depth of our data, for nine sources the CO J==3–2 emission remains undetected. We use a cube stacking analysis to recover average sample properties benefitting from the combined depth of the ALMA band 3 observations. We follow the methodology outlined in Geesink et al. (2026) to obtain stacked fluxes in discrete bins of stellar mass (M⋆M_{\star}), metallicity, SFR, specific SFR (sSFR), and the distance from the main sequence (SFR/SFRMS\text{SFR}/\text{SFR}_{\text{MS}}). The resulting stacked CO fluxes and the corresponding molecular gas masses derived from these detections are summarized in Table 4. We point the reader to Geesink et al. (2026) for a more detailed description of the cube stacking approach, especially the error-handling.

4 Analysis

4.1 ACE galaxies in context of literature compilations

To place the ACE galaxies in the context of the available information in the literature, we first show the distribution of properties of the ACE targets compared to the z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5 literature compilation in Figure 1. ACE has a relatively even distribution of metallicities between 12+log⁡(O/H)∼8.212+\log(\mathrm{O/H})\sim 8.2 and 8.68.6. The ACE sample newly probes lower metallicities, 12+log⁡(O/H)<8.512+\log(\mathrm{O/H})<8.5, than has been achieved for unlensed targets at cosmic noon thus far. The ACE sample is mostly centered at M⋆<1010.5​M⊙M_{\star}<10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}, with SFR\mathrm{SFR}s between 1010 and 100​M⊙​yr−1100\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}. This is a so far mostly unexplored regime in stellar mass and SFR\mathrm{SFR}. ACE increases the number of unlensed galaxies at z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5 for which both CO\mathrm{CO} and metallicity information are available by a factor of approximately 3. We compare the location of the galaxies in the stellar mass – SFR parameterization to the star-forming main-sequence presented by Popesso et al. (2023), which is based on a compilation of literature samples with SFRs predominantly obtained through SED fitting or from UV + IR emission. Most of the ACE galaxies lie within half a dex\mathrm{dex} of the star-forming main sequence (all except for two) and have sSFRs between 10−910^{-9} and 10−8​yr−110^{-8}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}.

The literature compilation, on the other hand, shows a significantly larger spread in SFR\mathrm{SFR}s, resulting in a wide dispersion in sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} and a substantial offset from the main sequence as well. The ACE sample shows a more normal distribution in most of the panels of Figure 1. This prominent difference in sample selection must be kept in mind when comparing the ACE galaxy properties to the literature compilation in all subsequent figures.

In Figure 2, we show the placement of the ACE targets with respect to the main sequence of star-forming galaxies at z∼2.3z\sim 2.3 as derived by Popesso et al. (2023). Most of the ACE galaxies are within ∼0.3​dex\sim 0.3\,\mathrm{dex} of the main sequence (see also Figure 1). A few of the galaxies, especially the two lowest-mass objects, are significantly elevated above the Popesso et al. (2023) main sequence by up to ∼1​dex\sim 1\,\mathrm{dex} for one of the targets. In contrast, the literature compilation shows a much larger scatter about the main sequence, with extremes extending up to an order of magnitude both above and below it.

4.2 Molecular gas scaling relations

In the next three subsections, we show the scaling relations between molecular gas mass and other galaxy properties, focusing specifically on Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and tdept_{\mathrm{dep}}. We show the individual and stacked measurements for the ACE sample. In all figures, we compare the ACE galaxies to the literature compilation with metallicity information, the Tacconi et al. (2020) compilation of galaxies with CO\mathrm{CO}-based molecular gas masses (assuming a fixed αCO\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}} conversion factor), and the z=0z=0 comparison sample from Galliano et al. (2021). The ACE galaxies, as well as the literature compilation with metallicity information, are all colour-coded according to their metallicity. Furthermore, we display the Kendall rank correlation coefficient in every figure to evaluate the degree of similarity between the two sets of ranks assigned to the same set of objects. We use the implementation presented in Flury (2023), which is based on the two-variable correlation formalism of Akritas and Siebert (1996) that accounts for censoring (upper/lower limits). We evaluated the Kendall rank correlation based on the combined set of ACE galaxies and literature compilation with metallicity information. In all plots, τ\tau denotes the degree of correlation, where 0 indicates no correlation, and increasingly positive (negative) values up to 1 (-1) represent a positive (negative) correlation. pp is the two-sided pp-value, indicating the probability of obtaining the observed correlation purely by chance (with smaller pp-values reflecting higher statistical significance). We present a full summary of the Kendall τ\tau correlation coefficient and corresponding pp-value for each relation plotted in this paper in Table 1.

4.2.1 Molecular gas as a function of stellar mass and SFR

We present the molecular gas mass of galaxies as a function of their stellar mass in the left panel of Figure 3. We find that the ACE galaxies with a CO\mathrm{CO} detection show a clear increase in their molecular gas mass with stellar mass of a dex over the stellar mass range from 109.510^{9.5} to 1010.5​M⊙10^{10.5}\,\rm{M}_{\odot}. The upper limits on molecular gas mass for targets without a robust CO\mathrm{CO} detection are entirely consistent with this trend, though admittedly the stack of the lowest stellar mass bin has a molecular gas mass similar to the central bin. The latter may seem surprising at first glance, but it can be explained by a selection effect: our sample in the lowest stellar mass bin is preferentially biased toward galaxies occupying the upper envelope of, or lying entirely above, the star-forming main sequence (Figure 2). Given the tight link between SFR and MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} (see Figure 3; right panel) this naturally drives a higher MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} for a fixed stellar mass. Overall, the ACE galaxies form a natural lower-mass continuation of the MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}–M⋆M_{\star} relation mapped out by the Tacconi et al. (2020) compilation. Crucially, the ACE sample probes galaxies down to an order of magnitude lower in stellar mass than probed before in unlensed galaxies at cosmic noon, demonstrating that this scaling relation persists down to at least M⋆∼109.5​M⊙M_{\star}\sim 10^{9.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}. The high-redshift literature compilation with metallicity information shows a significantly larger scatter in the MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}–M⋆M_{\star} plane, reflecting its broader distribution in properties such as SFR\mathrm{SFR}. We find a Kendall rank correlation coefficient of τ=0.26\tau=0.26 with a pp-value of ∼0.03\sim 0.03 for the combined ACE and literature sample, indicating a marginally significant positive correlation. The ACE galaxies possess molecular gas masses nearly a dex\mathrm{dex} higher than their local z=0z=0 counterparts at a fixed stellar mass. We find no secondary dependence on metallicity within the ACE sample; that is, the residual scatter in the MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}–M⋆M_{\star} plane is not explained by gas-phase metallicity.

The right-hand panel of Figure 3 displays the SFR\mathrm{SFR} of galaxies as a function of their molecular gas mass, representing the integrated molecular Schmidt-Kennicutt relation (Kennicutt, 1998; Daddi et al., 2010; Genzel et al., 2010). The ACE galaxies define a remarkably tight correlation, where the SFR\mathrm{SFR} increases robustly with molecular gas mass. The ACE galaxies follow a somewhat super-linear relation between molecular gas mass and SFR, corresponding to an average molecular gas depletion time (τdep\tau_{\mathrm{dep}}) just below 1​Gyr1\,\mathrm{Gyr}. In contrast, the stacked measurements show a slightly sub-linear trend toward higher molecular gas masses. The differing slopes inferred from the detections and stacks likely reflect selection effects and the incomplete sampling of the star-forming main sequence across the full parameter space. When combined with literature measurements, however, the overall relation extends smoothly over a broad range of molecular gas masses and remains consistent with an approximately constant depletion time, in agreement with the compilation of Tacconi et al. (2020).

Because the ACE galaxies sample a lower stellar mass regime than previous z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5 literature compilations, these data demonstrate that the integrated molecular Schmidt-Kennicutt relation extends to lower masses and lower star formation regimes. This tight scaling relation is reflected by a high Kendall correlation coefficient of τ=0.48\tau=0.48 with a pp-value of 4.3×10−54.3\times 10^{-5}, ruling out random chance as a driver. As with the relation between MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} and M⋆M_{\star}, we find no strong secondary dependence on metallicity to account for the intrinsic scatter in the MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}–SFR\mathrm{SFR} relation. The super-linear trend between SFR and MmolM_{\rm mol} connects continuously down to the scales probed by the local z=0z=0 comparison sample, suggesting that the underlying relation is largely redshift-independent. It is important to note that we do not control for sample matching between the z==0 and cosmic noon populations. Therefore, the observed change in the average depletion time should not be interpreted as evidence for redshift evolution, as it may instead reflect differences in the sampled galaxy populations, such as their position relative to the main sequence or their specific star formation rates.

4.2.2 The molecular-to-stellar mass ratio

In Figure 4, we show the molecular-to-stellar mass ratio (Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}) of galaxies as a function of their stellar mass, metallicity, offset from the star-forming main sequence (SFR/SFRMS\mathrm{SFR}/\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{MS}}), and sSFR\mathrm{sSFR}, respectively. We find a weakly declining trend between Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and stellar mass, with a Kendall rank correlation coefficient of τ=−0.28\tau=-0.28. This downward trend is also apparent in the Tacconi et al. (2020) and local z=0z=0 compilations, though it is less pronounced. Similarly, the stacked binned measurements of the ACE sample show a shallower trend than the individual galaxies. We find no secondary dependence on metallicity driving the scatter within the Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}–M⋆M_{\star} plane. We find that at fixed stellar mass, Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} increases with approximately an order of magnitude between z=0z=0 to z=2−2.5z=2-2.5, across the full stellar mass range probed. The two lowest-mass ACE galaxies have the highest molecular gas fractions (Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}), potentially suggesting a steeper increase of Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} toward lower stellar masses than inferred from the remainder of the sample. However, it is important to note that both galaxies lie significantly above the star-forming main sequence and may therefore not be representative of the typical galaxy population at these masses.

We observe a weak correlation between Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and gas-phase metallicity for the ACE galaxies, the cosmic noon literature compilation with metallicity information, and the stacked data, confirmed by a Kendall coefficient of τ=−0.09\tau=-0.09 with a pp-value of 0.460.46. This lack of a strong correlation is somewhat surprising, given the prominent decline in Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} as a function of increasing metallicity seen in the local z=0z=0 comparison sample. The differences may be driven by selection effects, both for the z=0z=0 sample and the cosmic noon galaxies. Indeed, the number of low-metallicity galaxies in Galliano et al. (2021) with CO measurement counterparts is very limited, restricted to the CO brightest (and thus most molecular gas rich) galaxies. Furthermore, we are not comparing samples that are complete in the multi-dimensional parameter space of stellar mass, SFR and metallicity at their respective redshifts. We do clearly find that the cosmic noon galaxies have higher Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} at fixed metallicity than the z=0z=0 compilation, with a typical difference of approximately 0.5 dex. This is in agreement with predictions by theoretical models (Popping et al., 2015; Lagos et al., 2015; Davé et al., 2020, e.g.,).

The bottom-left and bottom-right panels of Figure 4 demonstrate a clear positive correlation between Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and both the main-sequence offset and sSFR\mathrm{sSFR}, respectively, with Kendall values of τ=0.35\tau=0.35 (p=0.0045p=0.0045) and τ=0.30\tau=0.30 (p=0.0024p=0.0024). The presence of a star formation term on the xx-axis of both scaling relations underscores the tight physical coupling between SFR\mathrm{SFR} and molecular gas mass (as shown in the right panel of Figure 3). This robust positive correlation is also clearly visible in the stacked data points. We find no obvious secondary dependence on metallicity in either of these trends.

We find a distinct redshift evolution in Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} of approximately one dex from z=0z=0 to z=2−2.5z=2-2.5 at a fixed offset from the main sequence. The positive correlation between Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} on the other hand is redshift independent. The latter is a natural consequence of the tight relation between SFR\mathrm{SFR} and MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}, since Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} effectively share M⋆M_{\star} as a common denominator. The redshift evolution in Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} at fixed stellar mass can thus also be explained as an evolution in sSFR.

4.2.3 The molecular gas depletion time

We show the molecular gas depletion time of galaxies as a function of their stellar mass, metallicity, offset from the star-forming main sequence, and sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} in Figure 5. We find little to no trend between the depletion time of the galaxies and either their stellar mass or metallicity, yielding Kendall rank correlation coefficients of τ=0.00\tau=0.00 and τ=−0.03\tau=-0.03, respectively. This lack of correlation is also apparent from the stacked binned measurements. The depletion times of the ACE galaxies are centered around 1​Gyr1\,\mathrm{Gyr} (ranging from ∼300​Myr\sim 300\,\mathrm{Myr} up to ∼3​Gyr\sim 3\,\mathrm{Gyr}), in good agreement with depletion times previously found for more massive galaxies at these epochs (see the literature compilation with metallicity, as well as, e.g., Aravena et al. 2019; Tacconi et al. 2020). On average, the ACE galaxies have depletion times that are somewhat shorter than those found for the local z=0z=0 comparison sample.

There is a slightly more pronounced downward trend between depletion time and both the offset from the main sequence and sSFR\mathrm{sSFR}, with a Kendall coefficient of τ=−0.15\tau=-0.15 (p=0.19p=0.19) for both parameters. These trends are in good agreement with the Tacconi et al. (2020) compilation and are also clearly reflected in the stacked bins. This indicates that galaxies become increasingly efficient at forming stars as they move from below to above the star-forming main sequence. We find that at a fixed offset from the main sequence, the ACE galaxies have depletion times that are systematically shorter than those of z=0z=0 galaxies (with typical values of ∼1​Gyr\sim 1\,\mathrm{Gyr} versus ∼3​Gyr\sim 3\,\mathrm{Gyr}). Similar to the behaviour observed for Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}, there appears to be an underlying relation between sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} and tdept_{\mathrm{dep}} that holds across cosmic time, where galaxies with higher sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} have shorter gas depletion times.

4.3 Redshift evolution

We show the molecular-to-stellar mass ratio and molecular gas depletion time of galaxies as a function of redshift in Figure 6, colour-coded by their gas-phase metallicity and stellar mass. We find that Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} increases by approximately an order of magnitude from z=0z=0 to z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5. Conversely, the depletion time decreases slightly with redshift, by roughly a factor of three over the same cosmic timeframe. These results are in excellent agreement with previous evolutionary studies (Aravena et al., 2019; Tacconi et al., 2020, e.g.,).

Notably, this evolutionary trend has not previously been investigated for unlensed galaxies with stellar masses of M⋆<1010.5​M⊙M_{\star}<10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} and metallicities extending well below solar. We show for the first time that galaxies in this low-mass, low-metallicity regime follow the same redshift evolution in Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} between z∼2.3z\sim 2.3 and z=0z=0 as observed in more massive systems, while maintaining systematically higher molecular gas fractions at fixed redshift (Figure 4).

5 Discussion

5.1 What drives star formation in galaxies?

A central objective in studying galaxy assembly is understanding the fundamental drivers of star formation. Is an elevated SFR primarily driven by an increased supply of available molecular gas mass—the raw fuel for star formation—or by a fundamental shift in star formation efficiency? Furthermore, does this efficiency evolve as a function of stellar mass, gas-phase metallicity, different galaxy properties or time? In this paper, we present the molecular gas properties of 26 typical star-forming galaxies at z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5, observed with ALMA as part of the ACE large program. The defining feature of this sample is that it probes unlensed galaxies with stellar masses nearly an order of magnitude lower, and metallicities ∼0.4​dex\sim 0.4\,\mathrm{dex} lower, than previously achieved at cosmic noon by surveys such as PHIBSS (Tacconi et al., 2018) and ASPECS (Aravena et al., 2019). This opens up a new parameter space for investigating molecular gas and its link to the stellar buildup in typical galaxies at cosmic noon.

Our results support the view that molecular gas availability is the primary regulator of star formation. This is clearly demonstrated by the tight correlation between MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} and SFR (Figure 3; right panel), which is the most statistically significant relation identified in this work and underscores the fundamental role of molecular gas availability in driving star formation. Moreover, the smooth continuity of this relation between the ACE galaxies and z=0z=0 comparison sample suggests that its overall form is largely independent of redshift. Although the observed differences in average depletion times between cosmic noon and z=0z=0 could indicate evolution, they should be interpreted with caution, as the low- and high-redshift samples are not matched in their galaxy properties. Any apparent variation may therefore reflect differing distributions in specific star formation rate or position relative to the star-forming main sequence (Saintonge and Catinella, 2022), rather than genuine redshift evolution.

Consistent with the interpretation that variations in depletion time are primarily driven by galaxy properties rather than redshift, Figures 4 and 5 show that both the molecular-to-stellar mass ratio and molecular gas depletion time correlate most strongly with sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} and offset from the star-forming main sequence. These relations remain continuous across the combined z∼0z\sim 0 and z∼2z\sim 2 samples, further strengthening that sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} is closely linked to molecular gas fraction and depletion time across cosmic time. The prominent correlation with sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} and main-sequence offset, characterized by Kendall rank coefficients of τ∼0.35\tau\sim 0.35 for Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and τ=−0.15\tau=-0.15 for tdept_{\mathrm{dep}}, reveals two key physical insights. First, at fixed stellar mass, galaxies with elevated sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} (above the main sequence) possess larger molecular gas reservoirs, demonstrating that gas availability is the primary driver of enhanced star formation activity. Second, these galaxies also deplete their molecular gas more rapidly, implying higher star formation efficiencies than systems with lower sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} (below the main sequence). These trends remain coherent across a wide stellar mass range of 10910^{9}–1011​M⊙10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} and a gas-phase metallicity range of 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.212+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=8.2–8.88.8, indicating that variations in both gas content and star formation efficiency govern a galaxy’s position relative to the star-forming main sequence. However, the physical mechanisms responsible for the observed efficiency variations remain uncertain.

We find no significant correlation between molecular gas depletion time and gas-phase metallicity (top-right panel of Figure 5). One might expect that the reduced shielding against ionizing radiation in metal-poor environments would alter molecular cloud structures, rendering them less efficient at forming stars. Complementary work by Geesink et al. (2026) demonstrates that the dust-to-gas ratio increases with metallicity, and Popescu et al. (2026) find that dust temperatures systematically increase toward lower metallicities. Nevertheless, these prominent variations in interstellar medium properties do not appear to impact the conversion efficiency of molecular gas into stars across the entire metallicity regime covered by ACE. This unexpected invariance could be indicative of a relatively constant dense gas fraction (i.e., the dense molecular gas cores where star formation actually occurs), though confirming this scenario will require future observations of high-density gas tracers. We emphasize that this work focuses exclusively on the molecular gas budget. Because theoretical models predict a strong correlation between the fraction of cold gas in the molecular phase (fH2f_{\mathrm{H}_{2}}) and gas-phase metallicity (Krumholz et al., 2008; Gnedin and Kravtsov, 2010), one might expect a significantly more pronounced trend to emerge when considering the total cold-gas depletion time (including atomic hydrogen) of galaxies as a function of their metallicity. A caveat of our analysis is furthermore that the metallicities considered are derived from Hii region emission lines and therefore trace the ionized gas phase rather than the molecular gas itself. Implicitly, this assumes that the metallicity of the ionized gas is representative of that of the molecular gas. Any systematic differences between these phases could weaken intrinsic trends and may partly account for the lack of a significant correlation with metallicity found in our analysis.

Future analyses of spatially resolved gas, stellar mass and star-formation distributions of the ACE galaxies will be crucial for establishing how Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star} and tdept_{\mathrm{dep}} are connected to the underlying dynamical state and stability of galactic discs. Such observations will clarify the physical drivers behind the increased star formation efficiency observed as a function of sSFR, extending studies of more massive galaxies (Tacconi et al., 2020, see the review by).

5.2 Placing ACE in context: a comparison to lensed galaxies

This work presents some of the first constraints on the molecular gas content and depletion times of unlensed galaxies at cosmic noon spanning stellar masses of M⋆<1010.5​M⊙M_{\star}<10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} and gas-phase metallicities of 12+log⁡(O/H)<8.612+\log(\mathrm{O/H})<8.6. As discussed above, the scaling relations established for more massive and metal-rich galaxies appear to remain valid within this newly explored parameter space. However, it is important to account for the incompleteness of the ACE sample. As shown in Figure 2 and discussed by Shivaei et al. (2026), the ACE selection preferentially targets galaxies located on or slightly above the star-forming main sequence, particularly at low stellar masses and metallicities, and therefore misses galaxies in the lower envelope of the main sequence.

To place the ACE results into a broader context, we can compare them to studies of low-mass galaxies observed through gravitational lensing (Saintonge et al., 2013; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Sharon et al., 2019; Catán et al., 2024, e.g.,). The molecular gas fractions and depletion times measured for the ACE galaxies are generally consistent with those reported for lensed galaxy samples, suggesting that the gas scaling relations observed here extend into the low-mass and low-metallicity regime probed by ACE.

In Figure 7, we compare a compilation of lensed sources with metallicity and low-J CO information at redshifts z∼1.5−3z\sim 1.5-3 to the ACE galaxies and literature compilation with metallicity information. This compilation consists of all targets presented in Saintonge et al. (2013) and Catán et al. (2024), as well as A68-HLS115 (Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Girard et al., 2018), SDSS J0901+1814 (Sharon et al., 2019), MACS J0451+0006 (MACS J0451 Arc) (Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Curti et al., 2020), and RCSGA 032727-132609 (Rigby et al., 2011; Wuyts et al., 2014; González-López et al., 2017). When making this comparison, it is important to note that the stellar masses and SFRs of the lensed galaxies were derived using methodologies different from those adopted in this work. We recomputed the molecular masses presented in the respective papers using the metallicity-dependent calibration of Accurso et al. (2017) for consistency with the methodology employed throughout the ACE survey. 11 1 Catán et al. (2024) infer metallicities from stellar population modelling following Solimano (2022), adopting the simplifying assumption that the stellar and gas-phase metallicities are identical. No direct gas-phase metallicity measurements are available for these galaxies.

We find that the lensed galaxies broadly overlap with the ACE sample and follow the same general trends in molecular gas fraction and depletion time. At fixed stellar mass, the lensed galaxies are largely consistent with the ACE population and do not significantly broaden the observed distribution. However, when considering sSFR, the upper limits of the lensed sample push toward lower molecular gas fractions and shorter depletion times than the limits of the ACE sample. In Figure 7, we additionally report the Kendall rank correlation coefficients for the combined ACE, literature, and lensed galaxy samples. We find that both the resulting Kendall τ\tau values and the associated two-sided pp-values remain qualitatively unchanged compared to those listed in Table 1 for the ACE and metallicity-selected literature sample alone. This indicates that the inclusion of the lensed galaxies strengthens the explored parameter space without significantly altering the overall correlations.

This comparison between lensed and unmagnified galaxies highlights the importance of pursuing completeness across the full multi-dimensional parameter space of stellar mass, metallicity, and star-formation activity. Although ACE has opened a new window on the low-mass and low-metallicity galaxy population at cosmic noon, future surveys will require both greater sensitivity and more complete sampling of the star-forming main sequence to fully characterize the diversity of molecular gas properties in this regime.

5.3 Implications for galaxy formation theory

The observations presented here are of particular interest to cosmological galaxy formation simulations. These provide predictions for the (molecular) gas content and properties of large populations of galaxies across a wide stellar mass range, and robust observational constraints across the predicted mass range are thus essential for testing the physical processes that regulate the conversion of atomic gas into molecular gas and ultimately into stars (see Davé et al. 2020 for a comprehensive comparison of the cold gas properties of a number of cosmological simulations). The link to gas-phase metallicity is especially relevant, as many simulations adopt a metallicity dependent recipe to calculate the fraction of cold gas that is in a molecular form.

We find a weakly declining trend between molecular gas fraction, Mmol/M⋆M_{\rm mol}/M_{\star}, and stellar mass over the range probed by our data (Figure 4, top-left panel), in broad agreement with the behaviour predicted by several galaxy formation models (Lagos et al., 2011; Popping et al., 2015; Davé et al., 2020, e.g.,). We further find that galaxies in our sample follow the integrated molecular Schmidt–Kennicutt relation (right panel of Figure 3), linking molecular gas to SFR. This supports the use of the (resolved variant of the) relation as a star formation prescription in galaxy evolution models. Indeed, many semi-analytic and cosmological models assume by construction that star formation proceeds from the molecular gas phase following a variant of the Schmidt-Kennicutt relation (Somerville and Davé, 2015). The extension of the relation between molecular gas mass and SFR at cosmic noon down to lower stellar masses and metallicities, provides empirical support for this widely adopted framework. Note however, that more recent cosmological scale simulations have begun to explicitly model the formation of molecular hydrogen from first-principles (Ploeckinger and Schaye, 2020; Ragone-Figueroa et al., 2024; Schaye et al., 2026) and decouple the SFR from the molecular gas content (Schaye et al., 2026). This development enables the relation between molecular gas content and star formation to emerge as a genuine prediction of galaxy formation simulations, rather than being imposed by construction (see, e.g., Lagos et al. 2026). The observational results presented here thus offer important constraints for assessing the ability of these models to reproduce the physical processes governing galaxy evolution.

We find no strong dependence of the molecular gas depletion time on gas-phase metallicity (Figure 5, top-right panel). This result differs from the trends predicted by the COLIBRE simulations (Lagos et al., 2026), who find systematically longer molecular gas depletion times at higher metallicities at resolved scales. At the same time, our data reveal a clear dependence of depletion time on specific star formation rate (Figure 5, bottom-right panel), in qualitative agreement with the COLIBRE predictions Lagos et al. (2026). The apparent lack of a strong metallicity trend in the observations should nevertheless be interpreted with caution. First of all, the current work presents integrated properties, whereas Lagos et al. (2026) show resolved properties. Second, selection effects may significantly influence the observed parameter space and potentially obscure intrinsic correlations. A more detailed comparison between observations and theory, including a careful treatment of survey selection functions and detection biases, is therefore required.

5.4 Extending cold gas prediction relations to lower masses

The presented observations of unlensed cosmic-noon galaxies spanning a wider range of stellar masses and metallicities than published thus far provide an ideal opportunity to reassess molecular-gas scaling relations and derive updated prescriptions for predicting Mmol/M⋆M_{\rm mol}/M_{\star} across an expanded parameter space. This builds directly upon previous scaling frameworks, such as those presented by Liu et al. (2019), Tacconi et al. (2020), and Sanders et al. (2023). A key advantage of the galaxies presented in this work is the baseline homogeneity. As all H2\mathrm{H}_{2} masses in this work are derived using a uniform methodology (also for the derivation of gas-phase metallicities), our sample avoids the potential systematic effects introduced by mixing different gas tracers, such as the scaling relations of Tacconi et al. (2020) which rely on a combined compilation of both CO\mathrm{CO}- and dust-based molecular gas masses.

In Figure 3 we found a strong trend between MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} and SFR over 2 orders of magnitude SFR and cosmic time. We therefore adopt a functional form linking MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} and SFR to each other. In Figure 5 we found a weak dependence between sSFR and molecular gas depletion time and we therefore add sSFR as a second parameter. We fit log10⁡(Mmol)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{mol}}) using a Bayesian linear regression where the intercept, slopes, and intrinsic scatter (σ\sigma) are treated as free parameters. The posterior distributions are explored using MCMC sampling. For secure detections, we adopt a Gaussian likelihood that propagates asymmetric uncertainties in log10⁡(Mmol/M⋆)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}). CO\mathrm{CO} non-detections are incorporated as upper limits via a censored likelihood, ensuring that the true molecular gas masses are properly bounded. We exclude any literature galaxies with SFRs that classify them as quenched, defined here as lying more than 0.6​dex0.6\,\mathrm{dex} below the Popesso et al. (2023) main sequence. Our best-fit relation is given by:

log10⁡(Mmol/M⊙)=(0.94±0.03)​log10⁡(SFR/M⊙​yr−1)−(0.28±0.04)​log10⁡(sSFR/10−9​yr−1)+(9.09±0.04)\begin{split}\log_{10}\!\left(M_{\mathrm{mol}}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\right)&=(0.94\pm 0.03)\,\log_{10}\!\left(\mathrm{SFR}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}\right)\\ &\quad-(0.28\pm 0.04)\,\log_{10}\!\left(\mathrm{sSFR}/10^{-9}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}\right)\\ &\quad+(9.09\pm 0.04)\\ \end{split} (1)

with an intrinsic scatter of σ=0.20±0.02\sigma=0.20\pm 0.02 dex. Figure 8 shows the predicted molecular gas mass from this best-fit relation against the observed values, along with the corresponding residuals. We find good agreement across the entire probed range of MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}.

It is worth noting that metallicity is not explicitly included as an independent parameter in our fitting equation. Instead, it implicitly enters the relation through the combination of SFR and sSFR (which together connect directly to M∗\mathrm{M}_{*}). Because SFR\mathrm{SFR} and stellar mass are two of the primary parameters defining the Fundamental Metallicity Relation (Mannucci et al., 2010; Lara-López et al., 2010, FMR; e.g.,), the metallicity information is effectively encoded within these free parameters. A more detailed exploration of this, specifically focusing on the interplay between gas mass, metallicity, and stellar mass as a gas-based alternative to the FMR, is presented in Langan et al. (2026).

6 Summary

In this work, we presented a detailed study of molecular gas scaling relations in a sample of low-mass, low-metallicity star-forming galaxies at z∼2z\sim 2–2.52.5, observed as part of the ALMA Chemical Evolution (ACE) survey. By targeting CO J==3–2 emission in unlensed galaxies with stellar masses down to M⋆∼109​M⊙M_{\star}\sim 10^{9}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} and metallicities significantly below those of previous samples (8.2<12+log⁡(O/H)<8.68.2<12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})<8.6), we substantially extend the explored parameter space of molecular gas studies at cosmic noon. Combining these observations with a carefully homogenized literature compilation and consistent metallicity-dependent αCO\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}} estimates, we investigated how molecular gas content, gas fractions, and depletion times scale with global galaxy properties. The main findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    Molecular gas scaling relations at cosmic noon extend to M⋆∼109.5​M⊙M_{\star}\sim 10^{9.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}: The ACE galaxies follow the established MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}–M⋆M_{\star} and MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}–SFR relations, extending them down to at least M⋆∼109.5​M⊙M_{\star}\sim 10^{9.5}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} and metallicities of 12+log⁡(O/H)∼8.212+\log{(O/H})\sim 8.2. This demonstrates that the fundamental scaling relations identified in massive galaxies remain valid in the low-mass, low-metallicity regime at cosmic noon.

  • •

    Tight coupling between molecular gas and star formation: We recover a strong, slightly super-linear correlation between molecular gas mass and SFR. This relation has the tightest correlation in our analysis (τ=0.48\tau=0.48), indicating that the availability of molecular gas is the primary regulator of star formation activity.

  • •

    Offset from the main-sequence primarily driven by availability of molecular gas reservoir: The molecular-to-stellar mass ratio (Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}) correlates strongly with sSFR\mathrm{sSFR} and offset from the star-forming main sequence at fixed redshift, although showing only weak or negligible dependence on stellar mass and metallicity. This highlights that variations in the available gas reservoir are the dominant driver of elevated star formation rates at fixed stellar mass.

  • •

    Weak dependence of depletion time on galaxy properties: The molecular gas depletion time (tdept_{\mathrm{dep}}) shows little to no correlation with stellar mass or metallicity, and only a weak dependence on main-sequence offset and sSFR\mathrm{sSFR}. Typical depletion times are ∼1​Gyr\sim 1\,\mathrm{Gyr}, consistent with previous studies at similar redshifts.

  • •

    No strong metallicity dependence in observed scaling relations: We find no clear secondary dependence of MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}, Mmol/M⋆M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\star}, or tdept_{\mathrm{dep}} on metallicity. This suggests that, once molecular gas is formed, its efficiency in forming stars is largely insensitive to metallicity.

  • •

    Low-mass galaxies at cosmic noon follow established evolutionary trends: At fixed stellar mass, galaxies at z∼2z\sim 2 have molecular-to-stellar mass ratios nearly an order of magnitude higher than local galaxies, while depletion times evolve only weakly (by a factor of ∼2\sim 2–33). These trends persist down to the lower-mass regime uniquely probed by ACE.

  • •

    Refined fitting function for gas fractions: We derive an empirical prescription for predicting of MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} as a function of SFR and sSFR, with an intrinsic scatter of σ≈0.2\sigma\approx 0.2 dex.

Overall, our results reinforce a unified picture in which star formation in galaxies is primarily governed by the availability of molecular gas, while variations in efficiency play a secondary role. The key scaling relations linking gas, stars, and star formation remain remarkably robust across nearly two orders of magnitude in stellar mass and over a wide range in metallicity, suggesting a common physical framework underlying galaxy evolution.

The ACE survey opens a critical new window onto the molecular gas properties of typical progenitors of present-day galaxies. Looking ahead, expanding such studies to more complete and less biased samples, particularly toward lower main-sequence offsets and even lower metallicities, will be essential for fully characterizing the gas cycle across cosmic time. Future observations targeting dense gas tracers, spatially resolved gas distributions, and molecular gas dynamics will further illuminate the physical mechanisms regulating star formation efficiency. A significant step forward, especially at the low-mass faint-CO regime, will require a significant increase in the line-sensitivity of ALMA, offered for example by the ALMA2040 concept (Facchini et al., 2025). Ultimately, these efforts will be key to developing a complete picture of galaxy evolution that consistently links gas accretion, star formation, and feedback across all cosmic epochs.
